title: Match
intro: `match` is Rust's `switch` / `when`. It also returns a value, it must cover every possible value, and its patterns can take a value apart (a tuple, a list, a range).

coming_from.go: `match` is a `switch` with no fall-through, where `_` is `default`, `6 | 7` lists values, and `1..=5` matches a range. It must cover every possible value, and it gives back a value, so there is no `var kind string` to fill in.
coming_from.kotlin: `match` is your `when`: `_` is `else`, `6 | 7` is `6, 7`, and `1..=5` is `in 1..5`. It must cover every value even for an `Int` used as a statement, which Kotlin's `when` does not check. A pattern can also take a value apart (`(0, y)`, `[first, ..]`), which a `when` branch cannot.
coming_from.python: This is Python's `match`/`case`, with `|` and `_` meaning the same thing. The differences are that `match` gives back a value, and the compiler refuses to build if some value isn't covered.
coming_from.typescript: `match` replaces `switch`, with no fall-through and no `break`. Each arm gives a value, and the compiler checks that every case is covered, which is the `never` trick built in.
coming_from.java: `match` is a Java 21 `switch` expression with arrows: it returns a value and must cover every case. `6 | 7` is `case 6, 7`, `_` is `default`, and the range `1..=5` is a pattern of its own, where Java uses a `when` guard (on an `Object` or `Integer`).
coming_from.csharp: `match` is your switch expression: `1..=5` is `>= 1 and <= 5`, `6 | 7` is `6 or 7`, and `_` is the same discard. The real difference is that a missing case is a compile error in Rust, not a CS8509 warning followed by a runtime exception.
coming_from.c: `match` is a `switch` that returns a value and never falls through, so there is no `break`. The compiler refuses a `match` that misses a possible value, where C would quietly skip it.
coming_from.cpp: `match` is a `switch` with no fall-through that produces a value, plus ranges (`1..=5`) and alternatives (`6 | 7`). Leaving out a case is a hard compile error. In C++ a `switch` over an `int` with no `default` says nothing at all.

notes: Cases never fall through to the next one. There is no `break` to forget.
`|` means "or". `1..=5` is a range that includes 5; `1..5` stops before it.
A plain name in a pattern is a new variable that fits anything. It does not compare with a variable of the same name.
`match` gets much more useful with enums, Option and Result (lessons below).

gotcha.title: Leaving out the "anything else" case
gotcha.looks_fine: You know `day` is between 1 and 7, so a `switch` without `default` looks fine. In several of the languages here that is allowed: a day you did not list leaves `kind` empty, or fails later at run time.
gotcha.rust_sees: The compiler does not know what you know. It only sees that `day` is an `i32`, and an i32 can be 0, -5 or 99.
gotcha.why: This is a rule, not a safety proof. Nothing unsafe happens in the other languages: each picks what a missing case does (an empty string, an exception). For `day = 99`, which branch runs, and what is `kind`? Rust asks you to answer now, for every value, even the ones you think can't happen.

go.says: Go runs this and prints weekend. With `day = 99` no case would match, and `kind` would quietly stay an empty string.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints weekend. A `when` statement over an `Int` doesn't have to cover every value (over an enum, a sealed type or a `Boolean` Kotlin does check), so `day = 99` would quietly leave `kind` empty. Written as `val kind = when (day) { … }`, Kotlin refuses it, as shown further down the page.

python.says: Python prints weekend because 6 matches a case. With `day = 99` no case would match, `kind` would never be set, and the `print` would raise a NameError.
python.code:
day = 6
match day:
    case 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5:
        kind = "weekday"
    case 6 | 7:
        kind = "weekend"
print(kind)

typescript.says: TypeScript refuses this too (under `--strict`): the function promises a `string`, but when no case matches it falls off the end and would return `undefined`. The error does not say which case is missing.
typescript.error: main.ts(1,31): error TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not include 'undefined'.

java.says: Java refuses this too: a switch expression on an int needs a `default` branch, or javac says it does not cover all possible input values.

csharp.says: It prints weekend, but the compiler warns that the switch is not exhaustive (CS8509). With day = 9 it would throw a SwitchExpressionException at run time.
csharp.warnings: Program.cs(2,16): warning CS8509: The switch expression does not handle all possible values of its input type (it is not exhaustive). For example, the pattern '0' is not covered.

c.says: C does not check that a switch covers every value. Day 6 prints weekend, but day 9 would quietly print an empty line.

cpp.says: A `switch` without `default` is fine in C++, so this prints `weekend`. A day like 9 would leave `kind` as an empty string with no complaint.

go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	day := 6
	var kind string
	switch {
	case day >= 1 && day <= 5:
		kind = "weekday"
	case day == 6 || day == 7:
		kind = "weekend"
	default:
		kind = "not a day"
	}
	fmt.Println(kind)
}

python.code:
day = 6
match day:
    case 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5:
        kind = "weekday"
    case 6 | 7:
        kind = "weekend"
    case _:  # _ means "anything else"
        kind = "not a day"
print(kind)

match.py.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


def classify(n):
    match n:
        case 0:
            return "zero"
        case (1 | 2 | 3) as few:
            return f"few ({few})"
        case n if n < 0:
            return "negative"
        case _:
            return "many"


def ends(items):
    match items:
        case []:
            return "empty"
        case [only]:
            return f"only {only}"
        case [first, *_, last]:
            return f"{first} to {last}"


def place(p):
    match p:
        case Point(x=0, y=0):
            return "origin"
        case Point(x=0):
            return "on the y axis"
        case {"mode": m}:
            return f"a dict with mode {m}"


for n in [0, 3, 12, -1]:
    print(n, "->", classify(n))
print(ends([]), ends([7]), ends([1, 2, 3, 4]), ends((5, 6)), sep=" | ")
print(place(Point(0, 0)), place(Point(0, 4)), place({"mode": "fast"}), sep=" | ")
